problem_motivation.content: The paper is motivated by the anomalous bulk–monolayer Curie temperature behavior in VI3 and seeks a deeper theoretical explanation of finite-temperature magnetism and the role of interlayer coupling as its microscopic origin.
evidence_spans: aiming to identify the microscopic origin of the bulk–monolayer anomaly
This calls for a deeper theoretical investigation of finite-temperature magnetism in VI3 and the role of interlayer coupling.

problem_motivation.content: There is a gap in prior work on finite-temperature simulations: although LO and HO atom types have been proposed, simulations comparing their finite-temperature behavior separately and in mixture are missing.
evidence_spans:
Although basic properties of LO and HO atom types have been proposed,
a simulation comparing the finite-temperature behavior of these two types separately as well as in a mixture is
missing.

problem_motivation.content: The interlayer exchange/interlayer interaction in bulk VI3 is difficult to determine: no published calculation is available for the HO state, and qualified estimates are challenging because the interaction is highly sensitive to geometry and stacking.
evidence_spans: We are unaware of any published calculation of the interlayer interaction for bulk VI3 in the HO state.
This makes a qualified estimate of its value rather challenging.

problem_motivation.content: The regime where interlayer interaction is much weaker than intralayer interaction poses a significant challenge for spin-wave theory.
evidence_spans: Note that the regime with interlayer interaction much weaker than the intralayer one represents a significant challenge for the spin-wave theory [12].

prior_approach.content: First-principles/ab initio calculations predicted two types of V atoms (HO and LO) with strikingly different magnetic anisotropies, differing by more than an order of magnitude; published values from earlier studies were adopted as about 15.9 meV for HO and 0.4 meV (upper limit) for LO, and prior work also provided LO intralayer exchange parameters.
evidence_spans: These types have strikingly different magnetic anisotropies, predicted to differ by more than an order of magnitude.

For the SIA of V we adopt the published disparate values obtained by ab initio calculations, 15.9 meV for the HO type [22] and 0.4 meV (upper limit) for the LO type [41]. The three nearest-neighbor intralayer interactions for the LO case were taken from calculations by Gordon et al. [11].

prior_approach.content: Prior ab initio studies disagreed on the orbital ground state of VI3: several predicted the high-orbital-moment (HO) configuration as the ground state, whereas others found the low-orbital-moment e′g^2 (LO) configuration to be the ground state.
evidence_spans: The configuration with a high orbital moment (hereafter HO) has been predicted as the ground state by several ab initio approaches [22, 23];
however, other calculations found the low-orbital-moment e′ 2 g configuration (hereafter LO) to be the ground state [24].

prior_approach.content: A recent DFT+U study found competing insulating states in VI3/VCl3, close in energy (about 10–50 meV) and highly sensitive to symmetry-breaking lattice distortions; related work by Camerano and Profeta showed that sufficiently large optical Γ-point phonon displacements can switch the system onto a different electronic energy surface and stabilize a symmetry-broken a1g-occupied insulating state.
evidence_spans: a recent DFT+U study of VI3 and VCl3 found competing a1g- and e′ 2 or a1g1e′ g g g-based insulating states to lie close in energy (of order 10–50 meV) and showed that symmetry-breaking lattice distortions can strongly reorganize their relative stability and orbital char-acter [28]

A related sensitivity of the electronic state to lattice distortions has recently been investigated by Camerano and Profeta [28]. They showed that a sufficiently large displacement along an optical Γ-point phonon eigenvector can drive the system onto a different electronic energy surface and stabilize a symmetry-broken a1g-occupied insulating state.

prior_approach.content: The same distortion-biasing procedure had been used previously by the authors in their VBr3 study.
evidence_spans: this is the same procedure used in our earlier VBr3 study. [19].

prior_approach.content: A recent spin-wave-theory study on VI3 correctly predicted the bulk Curie temperature but reduced the monolayer Curie temperature to about 14 K.
evidence_spans: a recent study based on spin-wave theory on VI3, which correctly predicts TC for the bulk but reduces it to ∼14 K for 1ML [11]

prior_approach.content: Torelli and Olsen previously studied magnetic-order stability in a two-dimensional anisotropic Heisenberg ferromagnet with nearest-neighbor coupling J1 only and proposed an analytical formula for TC.
evidence_spans: Torelli and Olsen have studied magnetic order stability for a two-dimensional anisotropic Heisenberg ferromagnet with nearest neighbor interaction J1 only [43].

prior_approach.content: Mean-field theory predicts that TC depends linearly on the total interaction sum J0.
evidence_spans: The mean-field approach (MF) predicts the linear dependence of TC on the sum over all magnetic interactions with each site, J0 [46]:

prior_approach.content: Irkhin et al. developed a fluctuation-corrected self-consistent spin-wave-theory expression for TC.
evidence_spans: Studies of this problem within self-consistent spin-wave theory have led to a fluctuation-corrected self-consistent spin-wave-theory (FC-SWT) expression by Irkhin et al.[12].

prior_approach.content: Neutron spectroscopy and x-ray absorption/XMCD measurements indicated coexistence of both V orbital configurations; earlier studies modeled this with an assumed 50% HO/LO concentration and reproduced observations with sufficient precision.
evidence_spans: In this section we construct a minimal disorder model containing both V orbital configurations, whose coexistence has been indicated by neutron spectroscopy and x-ray absorption/x-ray magnetic circular dichroism measurements [26, 25].
Its authors have assumed, in both cases, a concentration of 50%, which has allowed the reproduction of observations with sufficient precision.

prior_approach.content: Analogous stacking sensitivity of interlayer exchange has been demonstrated in other van der Waals trihalides, although direct experimental confirmation in VI3 is still lacking.
evidence_spans: Although direct experimental confirmation of this effect in VI3 is still lacking, analogous sensitivity has been demonstrated in other vdW trihalides [8, 9, 49, 10].

prior_limitation.content: Mean-field theory is limited for quasi-2D/small interlayer-coupling regimes: its accuracy worsens at small J_L, it only partially captures the J_L dependence because it reduces exchanges to an effective sum over neighbors rather than distinguishing different couplings, and it cannot describe the Mermin-Wagner limit when both J_L and magnetic anisotropy vanish.
evidence_spans: The accuracy of this method is thus clearly worse for small JL. The mean-field approach obviously cannot handle the Mermin-Wagner behavior in the limit of vanishing both JL and magnetic anisotropy, where the correlation length diverges exponentially as T →0 [47].

Even in the quasi-2D case of relatively small JL mean-field appears to capture the dependence only partially. The big difference between these two couplings is not correctly taken into account by mean-field theory, which utilizes only an effective sum of all exchange interactions with neighbors.

prior_limitation.content: The homogeneous defect-free FC-SWT model neglects defect- and stacking-induced spatial variations in exchange interactions.
evidence_spans: This discrepancy is not unexpected since the fluctuation-corrected spin-wave expression assumes a homogeneous defect-free system and does not include defect- or stacking-induced spatial variations of exchange interactions.

rejected_alternative.content: The paper rejects characterizing interlayer coupling by only a few individual values (e.g., J′1–J′3), arguing that this is insufficient, and instead uses the summed effective interlayer interaction JL.
evidence_spans: Presentation of few individual values (as J′1 - J′3 ) is thus insufficient for understanding the interlayer relations. Therefore the best characterization of interlayer interaction is provided by their sum over all sites in one simulation cell layer, divided by the total number of such sites N; we denote its value as the effective total interlayer interaction JL:

rejected_alternative.content: Although TC could also be identified from heat capacity or Binder cumulant, the study rejects those alternatives in practice and instead uses the susceptibility peak as the criterion for TC.
evidence_spans: Although the magnetic transition can also be identified from other quantities, such as heat capacity or Binder cumulant, we use the peak position of the susceptibility as a practical criterion for TC.

rejected_alternative.content: The authors reject modeling the system as spatially segregated domains and instead treat it as a random mixture of two V types, because prior magnon-spectrum fitting models did not include segregation and showed signatures of disorder.
evidence_spans: Note that Lane et al. [26] and Hovančík et al. [25] have used the term domains, which can evoke spatial segregation of the two types. However, the model used to fit the magnon spectra does not contain any segregation, and in fact signatures of disorder are encountered [26]. Therefore modeling the problem as a random mixture of two V types appears to be appropriate.

rejected_alternative.content: The study does not perform explicit polaron simulations, despite their potential for greater quantitative accuracy, because they are extremely computationally demanding and are left for future work.
evidence_spans: Simulations with polarons would probably be able to describe this situation quantitatively even more accurately, but these are extremely numerically demanding. Therefore, we leave it for the future as a potential step in improving our model.

inspiration_source.content: The mixed-bond approximation is inspired by Yang et al.'s orbital-dependent superexchange picture.
evidence_spans: This approximation is motivated by the orbital-dependent superexchange picture discussed by Yang et al.[22].

causal_claim.content: Variation in the ratio/concentration of the two V configurations (HO vs LO/high-anisotropy vs low-anisotropy) causes a large change in the bulk Curie/ordering temperature; increasing the fraction of HO/high-anisotropy sites raises TC by increasing single-ion anisotropy, suppressing transverse fluctuations, and can shift the ordering temperature from roughly 24 K to 70 K, with the anisotropy contrast alone capable of nearly doubling TC even if exchange remains homogeneous.
evidence_spans: The anisotropy contrast strongly affects thermal stability: increasing the fraction of high-anisotropy sites raises the energy cost of transverse spin fluctuations and increases TC.
Our results show that variation of the ratio between different V types can cause a rather large change in TC.
Increasing CHO systematically increases the bulk ordering temperature, from approxi-mately 24 K in CHO = 20% to approximately 70 K in CHO = 80% .

The two possible configurations of V correspond to the lower and upper boundary of the SIA range shown in Fig. 2 , and the difference between them can therefore lead to a change of TC by almost a factor of 2.
Thus, even when the exchange network is kept homogeneous, replacing HO sites with MLH sites is sufficient to reduce the Curie temperature, as seen in Fig. 5(b).
In particular, the variation with anisotropy allows us to expect a large change in TC when the occupation of different types of V changes.
Our results show that variation of the ratio between different V types can cause a rather large change in TC.

causal_claim.content: A near 1:1 ratio of the two V types reproduces the experimental bulk Curie temperature.
evidence_spans: The experimental bulk value is reproduced when the ratio is close to 1:1

causal_claim.content: Because TC is highly sensitive to the HO/LO ratio, controlling the relative occupations of the two V configurations could tune the ordering temperature over a broad range.
evidence_spans: The sensitivity of TC to the HO/LO ratio suggests that the ordering temperature of VI3 could be tuned over a broad range by controlling the relative occupation of the two vanadium configurations.

causal_claim.content: HO and LO states have different orbital occupations and magnetic anisotropies; the high-momentum/HO states have exceptionally large anisotropy, and these electronic-structure differences can produce strikingly different intralayer and interlayer exchange interactions.
evidence_spans: As HO and LO solutions contain different orbital occupations, it may lead to strikingly different exchange interaction of both intralayer and interlayer types.
They also differ in magnetic anisotropy, which in fact reaches exceptionally high values for the high momentum states [22, 23].

causal_claim.content: Local lattice perturbations introduced by polarons can generate coexistence of high- and low-momentum states, causing V-site inhomogeneity; because interlayer exchange can change sign under small distortions, such polaronic disorder can also strongly cancel the average interlayer exchange.
evidence_spans: The existence of both high- and low momentum states in real samples and the resulting inhomogeneity can, in fact, be ascribed to the local lattice perturbations introduced by polarons.

However, the fact that it may change sign upon small distortion means that in the presence of polarons there will be a large cancelation on average, and this key feature is also captured by our model with two V types.

causal_claim.content: Higher single-ion anisotropy increases the Curie temperature monotonically, though sub-linearly and with saturation at large anisotropy; at very low anisotropy, magnetic order is stabilized mainly by interlayer coupling.
evidence_spans: Figure 2 shows that the critical temperature increases monotonically with K, but the dependence is sub-linear and would tend to saturate at larger anisotropy (above the examined range).
Note that for the minimum anisotropy (approaching the Heisenberg limit), the magnetic order is stabilized mainly by the interlayer interaction addressed in the next section.

causal_claim.content: Removing interlayer coupling destabilizes magnetic order and lowers TC, while increasing interlayer coupling shifts magnetization curves to higher temperature and raises the transition temperature; this strong TC sensitivity to interlayer coupling is consistent with the observed pressure dependence of TC in VI3.
evidence_spans: Its absence should therefore destabilize the magnetic order and reduce the critical temperature (TC).

As shown in Fig. 3(a), the magnetization curves shift systematically to higher temperature as JL increases. The corresponding transition temperature rises nearly monotonically over the full range of couplings considered, as summarized in Fig. 3(b).
This sensitivity due to interlayer coupling is also consistent with the experimentally observed pressure dependence of TC in VI3 [45].

causal_claim.content: Interlayer exchange is highly sensitive to structure and electronic configuration: twisting, stacking changes, thickness reduction, and pressure-driven changes in vdW spacing or stacking alter interlayer interaction paths, can strongly change interlayer coupling, and may even reverse its sign.
evidence_spans: In these cases, the geometry of individual layers is not significantly changed, but the different geometry of interaction paths between atoms of different layers will strongly affect the magnetic interactions between layers [5].
For example, in CrI3 even sign of the interlayer magnetic exchange changes when the system is thin enough, so that in a bilayer individual layers are antiferromagnetically coupled [6].
Different stackings lead to significant changes in interlayer coupling [7].
Pressure experiments are expected to affect mainly the vdW gap size and thus again the interlayer coupling.

The pressure effect can be further enhanced if it leads to stacking change, different stacking has been seen to again change the sign of interlayer interaction in CrI3 [8, 9], CrBr3 [10]. or VI3 [11].
The values obtained (Tab. 1) highlight its sensitivity also to the electronic configuration, as the sign also differs for the two cases considered.

causal_claim.content: An inhomogeneous V environment changes not just site identities but the topology, number, and connectivity of HO-HO, LO-LO, and HO-LO interlayer exchange pathways; because these pathways can have different strengths and even opposite signs, the interlayer exchange field becomes spatially nonuniform and frustrated, introducing competing magnetic channels that weaken coherent interlayer order and suppress the bulk ordering temperature while leaving intralayer ferromagnetism relatively robust.
evidence_spans: At the same time, the interlayer super-superexchange network is modified by the inhomogeneous V environment. It becomes spatially non-uniform and can contain competing exchange pathways, weakening coherent interlayer magnetic order while preserving robust intralayer ferromagnetic correlations.
Changing CHO also changes the number and connectivity of the exchange paths between layers HO–HO, LO–LO, and HO–LO.
Since these paths can carry different exchange strengths and, in some cases, different signs, the interlayer exchange field becomes spatially non-uniform.
Figure 6 shows that changing the concentration does not simply replace one type of V site with another; it reorganizes the topology of the interlayer exchange network.

As the fraction of low-orbital sites increases, low-orbital and mixed interlayer paths become more frequent. Because these V–I· · · I–V geometries involve different orbital characters, they can contribute differently to the effective interlayer exchange and introduce competing magnetic channels.
This frustration weakens the global magnetic coherence of the bulk crystal and suppresses the ordering temperature.

causal_claim.content: Allowing exchange to depend on the local V environment lowers TC beyond the effect of anisotropy contrast alone, especially in LO-rich compositions; by contrast, at high HO concentration the anisotropy-only and environment-dependent models converge because HO sites dominate the magnetic order and LO sites cannot sustain extended fluctuations on their own.
evidence_spans: When the exchange parameters are also allowed to depend on the atomic type, the original HO+LO model, the Curie temperature decreases more strongly, particularly in the LO-rich region (shown in both 4(b) and Fig. 5(b)).

On the other hand, at high CHO the two models approach nearly the same transition temperature. This indicates that the magnetic order of the system becomes dominated by HO sites in this regime, and LO sites cannot achieve extended fluctuations on their own sublattice.
Figure 5 shows the temperature-dependent normalized magnetization for the anisotropy-only control model (HO+MLH). As CHO decreases, the magnetization drop shifts to a lower temperature.

causal_claim.content: In the mixed system, interlayer coupling does not significantly increase TC relative to the monolayer because competing interlayer pathways in the heterogeneous bulk cancel or frustrate one another, whereas such competing pathways are absent in monolayers.
evidence_spans: For this mixture, the presence of interlayer interaction does not significantly increase the critical temperature compared to the monolayer case, where competing interlayer pathways are absent.

causal_claim.content: The arithmetic-average approximation for mixed-bond exchange is justified by orbital-dependent hopping: the relevant hopping contribution appears twice for HO-HO, zero times for LO-LO, and once for HO-LO, so the HO-LO exchange naturally falls midway between the two extremes.
evidence_spans: This approximation is motivated by the orbital-dependent superexchange picture discussed by Yang et al.[22]. This picture rests on the relatively stronger hopping between e′1 -a1g1e′g orbitals (see Eq. (2) and Fig. 3 of [22]). This hopping enhances the FM interaction for the a1g1e′1 occupied pair (HO-HO case), where it contributes twice, while it does not contribute for the e′g 2 pair (LO-LO) case. For the a1g1e′g 2 occupied pair (HO-LO) it contributes once, e.g. by half the difference between HO-HO and LO-LO.)

mechanism_principle.content: Out-of-plane single-ion anisotropy is a key stabilizer of finite-temperature ferromagnetism in layered/2D magnets: it raises the energy cost of transverse spin deviations, suppresses transverse fluctuations, opens a magnon gap, and thereby enhances thermal stability and increases TC. In the strict 2D limit, such anisotropy is required for long-range order by the Mermin-Wagner theorem.
evidence_spans: Due to the Mermin-Wagner theorem such truly 2D systems feature long-range magnetic order at sufficiently low temperatures only if magnetic anisotropy is present [3, 4]
A stronger out-of-plane anisotropy suppresses transverse spin fluctuations, opens a magnon gap, and therefore stabilizes the ferromagnetic state against thermal disorder.

Single-ion anisotropy increases the energy cost of spin deviations and thus controls the thermal stability of the ordered phase (enhances TC). The effect is particularly important in layered magnets, where reduced dimensionality makes the ordered phase more sensitive to thermal fluctuations.
Among the different properties of these two types, the variation of anisotropy plays a key role in finite-temperature magnetization.

mechanism_principle.content: The composition dependence of TC is governed in part by anisotropy contrast between site types: increasing the fraction of high-anisotropy sites raises the cost of transverse spin fluctuations and increases TC, whereas replacing HO with low-anisotropy MLH/LO sites lowers that cost and weakens the stability of the out-of-plane ordered state.
evidence_spans: increasing the fraction of high-anisotropy sites raises the energy cost of transverse spin fluctuations and increases TC

This behavior is expected because the fraction of MLH sites increases, and MLH sites have a single-ion anisotropy much smaller than that of HO sites. The reduced anisotropy lowers the energy cost of transverse spin fluctuations and weakens the stability of the out-of-plane ordered state.

mechanism_principle.content: TC reduction in the mixed-orbital/compositional system is not explained by anisotropy averaging alone. Coexistence of distinct local orbital environments and anisotropies perturbs the interlayer V-I...I-V super-superexchange geometry, making like-site and mixed-site interlayer exchange paths differ in strength and even sign. This creates a spatially non-uniform, frustrated interlayer exchange network with competing pathways; the resulting exchange inhomogeneity weakens coherent interlayer magnetic order while preserving strong intralayer ferromagnetic correlations, providing an additional mechanism that suppresses bulk thermal stability and lowers TC.
evidence_spans: These results show that the reduction of TC with decreasing CHO is not controlled by anisotropy averaging alone. The smaller anisotropy of LO sites weakens the local stabilization of the ordered moments, whereas the environment-dependent exchange modifies the connectivity of the HO–HO, LO–LO, and HO–LO exchange paths. As a result, the effective magnetic coupling becomes spatially non-uniform, further suppressing the bulk ordering temperature compared to that of the anisotropy-only model.

When two local orbital environments coexist, interlayer exchange channels are no longer equivalent: like-site and mixed-site paths can differ in both strength and sign. The bulk interlayer coupling therefore forms a spatially non-uniform exchange network rather than a single homogeneous field.

This provides a microscopic route for suppressing the bulk ordering temperature. In the homogeneous model, the presence of JL always enhances TC. However, in the mixed-orbital network, the spatial variation of J′ ij reduces the coherence of the interlayer exchange field while preserving strong intralayer ferromagnetic correlations.
It becomes spatially non-uniform and can contain competing exchange pathways, weakening coherent interlayer magnetic order while preserving robust intralayer ferromagnetic correlations.
This indicates that exchange inhomogeneity provides an additional mechanism for reducing the thermal stability of the bulk magnetic state.

This coexistence represents a highly complex problem, where the components respond differently to thermal fluctuations, mainly due to their different anisotropy. The geometry of V–I· · · I–V interlayer super-superexchange is also strongly perturbed and leads to competing interlayer exchange pathways. The interlayer exchange network becomes spatially non-uniform and frustrated.
The resulting concentration dependence TC(CHO) here reflects the competition between robust intralayer ferromagnetic correlations and frustrated interlayer coupling.

mechanism_principle.content: Interlayer exchange is intrinsically weak and highly sensitive to stacking/geometry because it is mediated across the van der Waals gap by extended V-I...I-V super-superexchange channels; nevertheless, even weak interlayer coupling in a quasi-2D ferromagnet promotes coherence between layers and suppresses critical fluctuations, so a pure 2D model that omits it yields a vertically shifted/lower TC relative to quasi-2D simulations.
evidence_spans: The interlayer exchange is mediated by extended V–I· · · I–V super-superexchange channels across the van der Waals gap [48] and is therefore relatively small and highly sensitive to changes in the interlayer geometry and stacking registry; different stackings can even reverse its sign [11].

This is the expected behavior of a quasi-two-dimensional ferromagnet: although the interlayer interaction is weak on the meV scale, it suppresses critical fluctuations and promotes coherence between neighboring layers.
The two graphs can be seen as vertically shifted with respect to each other; this can be ascribed to the interlayer interaction missing in the pure 2D model.

mechanism_principle.content: The commonly invoked explanation for enhanced magnetism in thinner samples is an electronic-structure-driven strengthening of intralayer magnetism, e.g. band flattening that satisfies the Stoner criterion; but in van der Waals materials, where different layers have limited influence on intralayer properties, this mechanism is less applicable.
evidence_spans: Still, it is typically connected with an associated change of electronic structure connected to intralayer magnetic properties, for example, the flattening of bands so that the Stoner criterion may become satisfied in a thin layer rather than bulk.
However, in vdW materials, the influence of different layers on intralayer properties is limited.

mechanism_principle.content: The favored orbital state is determined by a delicate competition among electron correlations, lattice distortions, spin-orbit interaction, and Kugel-Khomskii orbital ordering.
evidence_spans: The preference for either of these solutions depends on a delicate competition between electron correlations, lattice distortions, spin-orbit interaction, and the Kugel-Khomskii orbital ordering mechanism [27].

mechanism_principle.content: Using the susceptibility peak to identify the transition is justified because it coincides with the rapid loss of magnetization.
evidence_spans: This criterion is appropriate because the susceptibility shows a pronounced maximum at the transition, coinciding with a rapid loss of magnetization M.

hypothesis_statement.content: The bulk–monolayer VI3 Curie-temperature anomaly can be explained by the combined effects of single-ion anisotropy and exchange interactions in a system containing two types of V atoms (HO/LO configurations); specifically, anisotropy contrast together with spatially non-uniform or competing interlayer exchange, rather than weak interlayer coupling alone, governs the reduced bulk ordering temperature and the bulk–monolayer TC difference.
evidence_spans: Here, we use atomistic spin-dynamics simulations to study critical temperatures in VI3 from the combined perspective of single-ion anisotropy and exchange interactions, aiming to identify the microscopic origin of the bulk–monolayer anomaly. We consider a system composed of two V types with properties predicted by first-principles calculations.

Thus, the new contribution of the present work is to connect the established HO/LO coexistence picture to finite-temperature magnetic ordering by showing how anisotropy contrast and spatially non-uniform interlayer exchange affect TC, including the anomalous bulk–monolayer difference in VI3.

In this paper, we use atomistic spin-dynamics simulations to understand the behavior of critical temperatures in this system from the combined perspective of single-ion anisotropy and exchange interactions, with a focus on identifying the microscopic origin of the bulk/monolayer VI3 TC difference.
The comparison suggests that weak interlayer coupling alone is not sufficient to explain the reduced bulk ordering temperature of VI3.

Thus, the combined change of single-ion anisotropy and exchange interactions between the two possible V configurations allows us to propose parameters that describe both bulk and ML VI3 behavior (shown in Fig. 7).

Our findings emphasize that weak interlayer interactions in van der Waals magnets should not always be viewed as simple stabilizing perturbations; when they are spatially non-uniform or competing, they can instead suppress magnetic order.

hypothesis_statement.content: Bulk and monolayer VI3 critical-temperature differences can be explained by different concentrations of V atom types with different electronic configurations, and exfoliation may alter excess charge, polaron concentration, and hence HO concentration in the monolayer relative to bulk.
evidence_spans: We have found that the different critical temperatures of the bulk and ML samples could be explained by a variation of the concentration of V atom types with different electronic configurations.

The exfoliation used to obtain an ML VI3 [17] can lead to a change of the possible excess charge on the V atoms. Therefore, also the concentration of polarons and the concentration CHO may differ from the bulk value.

hypothesis_statement.content: A plausible polaron concentration in real VI3 could generate a balance of affected and unaffected V atoms comparable to that assumed in the model.
evidence_spans: To achieve a similar amount of both affected and unaffected V atoms, roughly 1 electron per 20 formula unit (f.u) is needed, which corresponds to the doping of 0.0125 electron per atom. Such doping appears to be plausible in real VI3 samples.

hypothesis_statement.content: Controlling the relative HO/LO occupation should enable wide tuning of the Curie temperature, by at least a factor of two.
evidence_spans: Our results further suggest that controlling the relative occupation of the HO and LO V configurations could tune the Curie temperature TC over a wide range, with at least a factor of two differences between its upper and lower limits.

evidence_result.content: Changing the ratio of the two V configurations (HO/LO) causes a substantial shift in the Curie temperature; finite-temperature magnetization behavior supports coexistence of the two V configurations in VI3.
evidence_spans: Our results show that changing the ratio of the two V types can cause a substantial shift in TC.
Thus, the finite-temperature magnetization behavior provides further support for the coexistence of two V configurations in VI3.
Thus, we have provided further evidence for the picture of two coexisting V configurations in VI3, this time on the basis of finite-temperature magnetization behavior.

evidence_result.content: A near 1:1 HO/LO ratio reproduces the experimental bulk Curie temperature; in the model this corresponds to an HO concentration of about 0.46, consistent with prior experimental indications of roughly 50% coexistence.
evidence_spans: The experimental bulk value is reproduced when the ratio is close to 1:1, consistent with two experimental indications of coexisting V configurations.
Comparing the bulk TC with the prediction allows us to determine Cbulk HO =0.46 within the assumptions of our model.

Our simulations predict that the bulk system has TC close to the experimental one for Cbulk HO = 46%. This finding is in good agreement with other experiments, where the concentration of 50% allowed the observations to reproduce.

evidence_result.content: The experimentally observed monolayer Curie temperature is matched by a slightly modified V-type ratio, requiring an HO concentration of about 0.76, possibly related to polaron concentration.
evidence_spans: The experimentally observed monolayer TC is obtained for a slightly modified ratio, which may be related to the polaron concentration.
Agreement with the experimentally observed TC = 60K for an mono-layer is achieved for CML HO approximately 0.76.

evidence_result.content: Multiple experiments indicate coexistence of HO- and LO-type vanadium in VI3: HO-type V was directly observed, LO-type contributions were needed to reproduce x-ray absorption/XMCD spectra, and neutron scattering also indicated coexistence.
evidence_spans: HO-type vanadium has been observed experimentally in VI3 samples, while inclusion of an LO-type contribution was required to reproduce the measured x-ray absorption and x-ray magnetic circular dichroism spectra [25].
This coexistence was also indicated in neutron scattering data [26, 25].

evidence_result.content: VI3 exhibits small lattice distortions away from the high-temperature structure and is susceptible to stacking faults; XPS also found significant V2+ content, argued to form polarons.
evidence_spans: VI3 undergoes small lattice distortions that lead to deviations from the high-temperature ¯R3 structure [18, 29, 30] and is also susceptible to stacking faults [31].
Furthermore, x-ray photoemission spectroscopy in VI3 has shown a significant presence of V 2+ atoms, which have been argued to form polarons here [32].

evidence_result.content: The Torelli-Olsen analytical formula reproduces the anisotropy (K) dependence of TC reasonably well, except at low anisotropy.
evidence_spans: The analytical formula apparently captures the change of TC with reasonable precision, the largest difference to our simulation of quasi-2D system occurring for a low anisotropy.

evidence_result.content: For weak interlayer coupling the bulk response approaches the monolayer limit, while strong interlayer coupling shifts the transition temperature to about 70 K; homogeneous-system calculations therefore show that TC can be significantly modified by single-site anisotropy and interlayer exchange across realistic parameter ranges.
evidence_spans: For the weakest interlayer coupling, JL = 0.14 meV, the bulk response approaches the monolayer limit. For the strongest coupling, JL = 0.95 meV, the transition is shifted to approximately 70 K.
The results show to what extent the critical temperature can be modified by single-site anisotropy and interlayer exchange.

evidence_result.content: FC-SWT yields Curie temperatures closer to experiment than mean-field theory, but still overestimates the experimental bulk value.
evidence_spans: The obtained values are closer to the experimental bulk value of about 50 K [18] than the mean-field result, but remain higher.

evidence_result.content: Second- and third-neighbor intralayer exchange interactions in VI3 are small and not significant compared with the other effects considered.
evidence_spans: Notably, the 2nd and 3rd nearest-neighbor interactions appear to be small in VI3 and do not play a significant role compared to other effects considered here.

evidence_result.content: In mixed HO/LO configurations, the magnetization drops rapidly near the transition and the susceptibility shows a clear peak at the ordering temperature.
evidence_spans: In Fig. 4(a), the temperature-dependent normalized magnetization and susceptibility are shown for the representative mixed configuration with various concentrations CHO. The magnetization decreases rapidly in the transition region, whereas the susceptibility shows a clear peak at the ordering temperature.

evidence_result.content: Anisotropy contrast alone produces only a moderate TC slope, implying anisotropy is important but exchange-related effects are also needed; correspondingly, the bulk-monolayer TC difference decreases as HO concentration decreases, and for CHO < 0.4 the monolayer TC exceeds the bulk TC.
evidence_spans: The relatively moderate slope of the HO+MLH curve indicates that anisotropy contrast alone significantly changes the transition temperature, but exchange-related effects are also important.

Note that the difference between bulk and ML TC (shown in Fig. 4(b)) decreases with decreasing CHO, and therefore the stabilization due to intralayer exchange is less relevant as the competition between LO and HO type interaction becomes more balanced. For CHO < 0.4 the ML TC is even becoming higher than that of bulk.

evidence_result.content: Surface-sensitive spectroscopy shows stronger a1g occupation at surfaces, consistent with a higher HO concentration outside the bulk.
evidence_spans: Note that a comparison of surface and bulk-sensitive spectroscopies has revealed that occupation of the a1g level is more pronounced on surfaces [24, 50], again indicating volatility of the HO/LO concentration and probably higher concentration of the VI3 HO state when not in bulk.

constraint.content: To model quasi-2D VI3, the calculations neglect boundaries and interactions between non-neighboring layers, assuming translational invariance along the c axis so that exchange interactions are equivalent for all layers; this is justified because interlayer exchange is much weaker than intralayer exchange.
evidence_spans:
Because the interlayer exchange is much weaker than the
intralayer exchange, interactions between non-neighboring layers are neglected.

In a quasi-2D system, boundaries may be neglected and the exchange
interactions are equivalent for all layers due to the translational invariance along the c axis.

constraint.content: Because HO and LO are nearly degenerate and coupled to slightly different local lattice distortions, the calculations are biased toward one solution or the other by introducing small initial trigonal distortions before self-consistency.
evidence_spans:
Because these two occupations are nearly degenerate but coupled to slightly
different local lattice distortions (a Jahn-Teller/Kugel-Khomskii-type effect), we bias the calculation toward one
solution or the other by starting from a slightly modified trigonal distortion associated with each configuration, and
let the calculation reach self-consistency with the same DFT+U+SOC Hamiltonian;

constraint.content: The exact HO/LO concentration cannot be determined precisely from the key experimental methods used in the cited studies.
evidence_spans: The methods used in the key studies [26, 25] do not allow for a precise determination of the HO/LO type concentration.

contradiction.content: Monolayer VI3 was reported to have a higher Curie temperature than bulk (about 60 K vs 50 K), contrary to the usual expectation that reduced thickness and weaker interlayer coupling should lower TC.
evidence_spans: VI3 also shows an unusual thickness dependence: the reported monolayer Curie temperature, TC, is higher than that of the bulk, contrary to the usual expectation that interlayer coupling reinforces magnetic order.

Interestingly, an exception to this observation has recently been found in VI3, where 1ML TC reaches 60 K [17]
compared to the bulk TC of 50 K [18].

contradiction.content: The reported enhancement of TC in monolayer VI3 conflicts with a recent spin-wave-theory study, which matched the bulk TC but predicted a much lower monolayer TC of about 14 K.
evidence_spans:
This finding is in striking contrast to a recent study based on spin-wave theory on VI3, which correctly predicts TC for the bulk but reduces it to ∼14 K for
1ML [11].
